rejected_rivals.reason: Bazin reaches a slightly lower pre-cut chi2 per point (0.182 vs 0.369 for SALT3) but only by overfitting: it spends 5 free parameters per band on 9 (g) and 7 (r) detections that are ALL pre-maximum, so tau_fall and the plateau term are fixed by nothing in the data and the post-peak extrapolation is arbitrary. It is also a smooth single-exponential decline with no physical content, so it cannot produce the ztfr secondary maximum (the ~25-day shoulder) that a SN Ia must show and that dominates the r-band held-out points. Bands are fitted independently, so it carries no colour/SED information and cannot enforce a common explosion date. SALT3, by contrast, is a trained spectral time series whose post-peak shape is determined once the pre-peak rise fixes t0, x1 and the amplitude; it fits the pre-cut data acceptably (chi2/pt 0.37) with only 4 free parameters shared across bands. Bazin is also outside the submittable scope for this item.

Same objection as Bazin, more so: Villar adds a plateau/knee parameter (gamma) on top of the rise and fall timescales, i.e. 6 per-band parameters against 7-9 strictly pre-maximum points. Its pre-cut chi2 per point (0.182) is indistinguishable from Bazin's, confirming the extra freedom buys nothing the data constrain; gamma and tau_fall are entirely unconstrained here and the model would be a blind extrapolation over the whole graded window. Villar's shape is designed for core-collapse plateaus; the data give no evidence for a plateau object (see the SN Ia reasoning in notes), and it also cannot reproduce the r-band secondary maximum. Independent per-band fits again discard the colour information that is the main lever for redshift and extinction here. Outside the submittable scope for this item.

Used only as evidence, not adopted. Its encoding of these data is a clearly worse forward model: pre-cut chi2 per point 4.70 (g 6.02, r 3.00) versus 0.37 for SALT3, i.e. it does not even reproduce the data it was shown. Its latent redshift (0.276) and t0 (59738.2, before the last rising pre-cut detection, which is manifestly wrong since the object is still brightening at 59741.2) are inconsistent with the light curve. This is expected given the stated checkpoint limitations: trained on BTS light curves truncated at most 3 nights after first detection with no redshift information, so it has seen almost no photometry at the phases that will be graded and its amplitude/redshift degeneracy is unbroken. It is also not submittable for this item. Its one useful contribution was negative: it offers no support for a non-Ia interpretation.

notes: Object is a normal SN Ia caught ~14 observer-days pre-maximum and still rising at the cut. Evidence: smooth monotonic rise of 1.3 mag in 8 days; blue and slowly reddening g-r (-0.38 at 59736 to -0.19 at 59740); deep g non-detections at 59726.3 (20.90, 20.96) bracketing an explosion date ~17-18 rest-frame days before the fitted t0, which is the canonical SN Ia rise time; and SALT3 fits all 16 detections in both bands with 4 parameters at chi2/pt = 0.37. Redshift: the pre-cut chi2 is essentially flat in z (0.368-0.391 over 0.04-0.28), so z is not constrained by shape alone. I broke the degeneracy with the Hubble-diagram self-consistency of the fit itself: for each fixed z I formed m_B = -2.5log10(x0)+10.635 and the standardized M = -19.36 - 0.14*x1 + 3.1*c, then the implied z from mu (flat LCDM, H0=70, Om=0.3). The map has a fixed point at z_fit = 0.14 -> z_implied = 0.142; z=0.10 implies 0.136 and z=0.19 implies 0.148, so the solution is stable. Adopted z = 0.14. x1 and c are only weakly constrained by pre-peak data (formal errors 3.1 and 0.08); I checked the alternatives (x1 = 0.55, c = -0.12 at z = 0.14, and the free-z solution z = 0.185, t0 = 59747.6, x1 = 0.88, c = -0.179) and they differ from the submitted model by under 10 percent in flux everywhere in the graded window, so the answer is not sensitive to that choice, and I kept the maximum-likelihood values at the self-consistent redshift. Predicted behaviour: peak near 59747 at g = 19.06, r = 19.24, then a normal decline with the r-band secondary maximum keeping r bright (r = 20.18 at 59772, 21.08 at 59792). Phase coverage is safe: the first pre-cut detection is at rest phase -13 and the horizon at rest phase +40, both inside SALT3's -20 to +50 range, so no zero-flux truncation occurs. MW dust (E(B-V) = 0.02979) was fixed in the fit and is re-applied by the grader. DECLINE was considered and rejected: SALT3 is an adequate forward model here, fitting both bands to well under 1 chi2 per point with a physically sensible rise time, colour and standardized luminosity.
